items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1976-02-19
items.q: Jimmy Noon is a good illustration of this.

ctx.x: Well, now in this question of jazz and defining it, don't you think one of the problems that not only critics, but anyone who's discussing the art form has, is that jazz flourished, I guess you could say, in New Orleans for a period of, what, 20 years or something like that. And then all of a sudden it, you know, by 1920, things began to change, at least as the music carried itself outside of New Orleans. And it went through different, I guess you would term different stylistic changes. I mean, the form remained,…

The form remained, the style changed, and when the style did change, its normal process of change was rarely, if ever, based on fundamental aesthetic developments. But usually, and I would say possibly invariably, on social and economic ground. So that the concept, for instance, of Chicago jazz, I use words like that in quotes, but Chicago jazz did not come about because somebody ever had a new idea. But it came about because of the fact that it was forced to come about by historical circumstances. For instance,…
So, that you would say that the, would you attribute the rise of the solo as a dominant form to this kind of thing?
In this town, how did prohibition affect the saloon business? Oh, here it didn't affect anything. Oh, really?

Really, because nobody even, I don't, I don't think they even knew about it. Certainly nobody stopped drinking, nobody stopped selling booze, and nobody tried to enforce anything. Yeah. This was, uh, and nobody, no federal, except on a couple of occasions they came in and did token raids, but it didn't mean anything, because everybody knew that they couldn't deal with it here. Yeah. So, uh, however it had a big difference, made a big difference in the music business, especially in Chicago, where, at the beginning…
